summary: Panic when decoding malformed Ed25519 keys from Base64
details:
In version 0.11.1 and earlier of vodozemac, Ed25519PublicKey::from_base64() and
Ed25519SecretKey::from_base64() panic on malformed input instead of returning an
error, if the input decodes to 31 or 33 bytes instead of the expected 32 bytes.
An attacker who can supply a key to an application using vodozemac can crash it.

## Impact

Ed25519 public keys are routinely received from other Matrix users and servers,
so a malicious party can publish a crafted key that crashes clients parsing it.

The impact is limited to denial of service; no key disclosure or signature
forgery is possible.

Versions 0.11.0 and 0.11.1 of vodozemac have degraded secret zeroization
capabilities, due to changes in third-party cryptographic dependencies
(chacha-20poly1305, sha2, hmac), which moved secret zeroization capabilities
behind a feature flag while vodozemac disabled the default feature set.

## Impact

The degraded zeroization capabilities could result in the production of more
memory copies of encryption secrets and secrets could linger in memory longer
than necessary. This marginally increases the risk of sensitive data exposure.

In version 0.11.1 and earlier of vodozemac, the Olm root key ratchet did not
zeroize its HKDF output after use. Each ratchet step left a copy of the new root
key and chain key in freed heap memory.

## Impact

An attacker who can read the process's memory, for example through a separate
memory-disclosure bug, a core dump, or swapped-out pages, may recover root keys
and chain keys from earlier ratchet steps. A leaked chain key allows decrypting
the messages in that chain, weakening Olm's forward secrecy for affected
sessions.

summary: Usage of non-constant time base64 decoder could lead to leakage of secret key material
details:
Versions before 0.7.0 of vodozemac use a non-constant time base64 implementation
for importing key material for Megolm group sessions and `PkDecryption` Ed25519
secret keys. This flaw might allow an attacker to infer some information about
the secret key material through a side-channel attack.

## Impact

The use of a non-constant time base64 implementation might allow an attacker to
observe timing variations in the encoding and decoding operations of the secret
key material. This could potentially provide insights into the underlying secret
key material.

The impact of this vulnerability is considered low because exploiting the
attacker is required to have access to high precision timing measurements, as
well as repeated access to the base64 encoding or decoding processes.
Additionally, the estimated leakage amount is bounded and low according to the
referenced paper[[1]].

[1]: https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.04600

Versions 0.5.0 and 0.5.1 of vodozemac have degraded secret zeroization capabilities,
due to changes in third-party cryptographic dependencies (the Dalek crates),
which moved secret zeroization capabilities behind a feature flag while
vodozemac disabled the default feature set.

## Impact

The degraded zeroization capabilities could result in the production of more
memory copies of encryption secrets and secrets could linger in memory longer
than necessary. This marginally increases the risk of sensitive data exposure.

Overall, we consider the impact of this issue to be low. Although cryptographic
best practices recommend the clearing of sensitive information from memory once
it's no longer needed, the inherent limitations of Rust regarding absolute
zeroization reduce the practical severity of this lapse.
